records.name: Cottontail Rabbit
records.diet: Grasses and clover in summer; twigs, bark, and buds in winter
records.shelter: Rests in shallow grass 'forms'; uses brush piles and old burrows
records.preferredHabitat: Meadows and field edges with brushy fencerows to bolt into
records.fact: Cottontails rest in shallow ground depressions called 'forms' rather than digging their own burrows.

requirements.hint: Plant native grass and a berry bush, with shrub cover close by.

records.role: An abundant grazing herbivore and cornerstone prey animal of the meadow. It feeds on grasses, clover, and woody browse and breeds rapidly to offset heavy predation. Foxes, hawks, owls, and badgers all depend on cottontails as a food source.

records.name: Monarch Butterfly
records.diet: Caterpillars eat only milkweed; adults sip flower nectar
records.shelter: Roosts in trees and shrubs; overwinters clustered in dense groves
records.preferredHabitat: Open meadows and roadsides with milkweed and nectar flowers
records.fact: Monarchs migrate up to 3,000 miles, but no single butterfly makes the whole round trip; it takes several generations.

requirements.hint: Wildflowers plus dedicated butterfly flowers with milkweed.

records.role: A milkweed specialist and iconic pollinator whose caterpillars sequester the plant's cardenolide toxins, making both larvae and adults poisonous to most predators. Their bright orange warning coloration keeps nearly all birds and mammals away, so they have very few predators. Adults are important late-season nectar visitors.

sources.name: PNAS — Cardenolide sequestration and toxicity in monarchs

records.name: Song Sparrow
records.diet: Insects and invertebrates in summer; seeds and fruits year-round
records.shelter: Cup nest hidden on the ground or low in shrubs and grass tussocks
records.preferredHabitat: Brushy edges, weedy fields, and marsh edges with singing perches
records.fact: A male Song Sparrow can learn up to about 20 different tunes and sing hundreds of variations of them.

requirements.hint: Shrubs, native grass, and somewhere high to sing from.

records.role: A ground-foraging omnivore that switches between insects in the breeding season and seeds/fruit the rest of the year, so it both controls insects and disperses seeds. Its abundance makes it a key prey item for meadow hawks and snakes, linking ground invertebrates to larger predators.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds — Song Sparrow Life History

records.name: Mule Deer
records.diet: Browses shrubs, forbs, twigs, buds, and seasonal grasses
records.shelter: Beds in brushy cover, tall grass, or forest edges; no permanent den
records.preferredHabitat: Open meadows and shrublands with browse and water nearby
records.fact: Mule deer are named for their oversized, mule-like ears, which rotate independently to pinpoint the direction of danger.

requirements.hint: A healthier meadow with plenty of browse and a pond to drink from.

records.role: A large grazing herbivore that shapes meadow vegetation by browsing shrubs and forbs. Its grazing and droppings help cycle nutrients and keep browse in check. Its usual predators (coyotes, mountain lions) are absent from this meadow roster, so it faces little predation here.

sources.name: Landmark Wildlife — Mule Deer ears and senses

records.name: Red Fox
records.diet: Voles, rabbits, squirrels, birds, and insects; also berries and carrion
records.shelter: Digs earthen dens or enlarges burrows; uses brush and hollows
records.preferredHabitat: Meadows, farmland edges, and hedgerows across open country
records.fact: When 'mousing,' red foxes tend to pounce facing magnetic northeast, apparently using Earth's magnetic field as a rangefinder to judge the leap.

requirements.hint: Foxes only return once smaller animals are back, with denning cover and a balanced meadow.

records.role: A generalist mesopredator that helps control rodent and rabbit populations, hunting by stalk-and-pounce and rounding out its diet with insects, berries, and carrion. With larger predators like coyotes absent from this roster, it sits near the top of the meadow food web.

sources.name: Phys.org — Predation by foxes aided by Earth's magnetic field

records.name: Meadow Vole
records.diet: Herbivore; grasses, sedges, seeds, roots, and bark in winter
records.shelter: Shallow burrows and grass nests linked by surface runways
records.preferredHabitat: Moist grassy meadows and fields with dense ground cover
records.fact: Voles mow narrow 'runways' through the grass — tidy little highways they patrol between burrow openings.

requirements.hint: Any thick grass cover will do — voles arrive early.

records.role: A keystone prey species and prolific breeder that converts meadow plants into food for nearly every predator. Its grazing and runway-building shape the grass layer. Its abundance drives the populations of hawks, owls, foxes, snakes, and badgers.

records.name: Ground Squirrel
records.diet: Mostly seeds, grasses, and flowers, plus insects like grasshoppers
records.shelter: Extensive multi-entrance burrow systems dug in open ground
records.preferredHabitat: Open grassy meadows and slopes near rocky lookout points
records.fact: Facing a rattlesnake, these squirrels kick sand and wave heated tails — flushing their tails with blood to jam the snake's infrared 'vision.'

requirements.hint: Grass to eat and rocks to keep watch from.

records.role: A burrowing omnivore whose diggings aerate soil and whose abandoned burrows shelter other species. It eats seeds, greens, and insects and is major prey for hawks, foxes, snakes, and badgers. Its colonies anchor the meadow's rodent-based food web.

sources.name: PNAS — Ground squirrels heat their tails to discourage rattlesnake attack
The Ethogram (UC Davis) — California ground squirrel

records.name: Garter Snake
records.diet: Earthworms, amphibians, slugs, small fish, insects, and small rodents
records.shelter: Shelters under rocks and logs; overwinters in communal dens
records.preferredHabitat: Moist meadows and grasslands near sunny rocks and water
records.fact: Garter snakes are mildly venomous to their tiny prey but completely harmless to people.

requirements.hint: Warm rocks, grass to hunt in, and small prey already about.

records.role: A common meadow mesopredator that hunts earthworms, amphibians, fish, insects, and small rodents, using mild venomous saliva to subdue small prey. It helps control invertebrate and amphibian populations. It is preyed on by hawks, owls, and foxes.

sources.name: U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service — Common Garter Snake

records.name: Bumblebee
records.diet: Nectar for energy and pollen for protein, from many flower types
records.shelter: Nests in abandoned rodent burrows, grass tussocks, or ground cavities
records.preferredHabitat: Flower-rich meadows and grasslands with continuous bloom
records.fact: Bumblebees 'buzz pollinate' — vibrating their flight muscles to shake pollen loose from flowers like tomatoes and blueberries.

requirements.hint: The more kinds of flowers, the better.

records.role: A generalist, large-bodied pollinator that visits a huge variety of flowers for nectar and pollen. Its buzz pollination unlocks pollen that many other bees cannot reach, making it vital to meadow plant reproduction. It is preyed on by ambush hunters and aerial insectivores.

records.name: Grasshopper
records.diet: Herbivore feeding on grasses, sedges, and broadleaf forbs
records.shelter: Shelters in grass and low vegetation; lays eggs in soil
records.preferredHabitat: Sunny grasslands and meadows rich in grasses and forbs
records.fact: Grasshoppers hear through tympana — eardrum-like membranes on the first segment of the abdomen, not their heads.

requirements.hint: Grasshoppers return almost as soon as the grass does.

records.role: A dominant plant-eater and the meadow's key prey base, converting grasses and forbs into food for a huge range of predators. Its abundance supports birds, snakes, mammals, and other insects. Booms in grasshopper numbers ripple up the whole food web.

sources.name: Ecology and Evolution — Grasshopper diet (gut-content sequencing)

records.name: Lady Beetle
records.diet: Predator of aphids and other small, soft-bodied insects
records.shelter: Overwinters in leaf litter and aggregations; shelters on foliage
records.preferredHabitat: Meadows and gardens with aphid-infested plants
records.fact: A single lady beetle can eat around 5,000 aphids over its lifetime — roughly 50 a day.

requirements.hint: Flowers bring aphids, and aphids bring lady beetles.

records.role: A voracious small predator that controls aphids and other soft-bodied pests as both larva and adult, making it a valuable biological-control insect. In turn it is eaten by insectivorous birds and larger insect predators, linking the aphid layer up into the food web.

sources.name: UC ANR — Lady beetle aphid consumption

records.name: Western Meadowlark
records.diet: Mostly insects in summer (beetles, grasshoppers); seeds and grain in winter
records.shelter: Domed grass nest woven on the ground, often with a covered runway
records.preferredHabitat: Wide native grasslands and meadows with song perches
records.fact: The Western Meadowlark's flute-like song is the state bird anthem of six U.S. states.

requirements.hint: Meadowlarks need real expanses of native grass before they will nest, with a basin to drink and bathe.

records.role: A grassland omnivore that eats large numbers of grasshoppers, crickets, and beetles in summer while taking seeds in winter, helping keep insect populations in check. As a plump ground bird it is important prey for hawks and mammalian predators of the meadow.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds — Western Meadowlark

records.name: Barn Swallow
records.diet: Flying insects caught midair: flies, beetles, bees, wasps, and moths
records.shelter: Cup nest of mud pellets and grass on beams under eaves and bridges
records.preferredHabitat: Open country for foraging near water, flowers, and structures
records.fact: Barn Swallows build their cup nests from up to 1,000 individual beakfuls of mud.

requirements.hint: A pond for mud and insects, and a perch to rest between flights.

records.role: An aerial insectivore that snaps up huge numbers of flying insects over meadows, following livestock and machinery to catch flushed prey. It is a natural check on flies and flying pests, and both adults and fledglings are hunted by fast-flying hawks.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds — Barn Swallow Life History

records.name: Red-tailed Hawk
records.diet: Mostly small mammals (voles, ground squirrels, rabbits); also birds and snakes
records.shelter: Bulky stick nest in the crown of a tall tree or on a cliff ledge
records.preferredHabitat: Open country: grasslands, fields, and meadows seen from above
records.fact: That piercing 'eagle' cry in the movies is almost always actually a Red-tailed Hawk.

requirements.hint: Hawks watch for a meadow already full of small animals.

records.role: The meadow's apex daytime hunter, soaring on broad wings or watching from a perch for prey below. By preying on voles, ground squirrels, rabbits, and birds it keeps herbivore numbers in check. Adults have essentially no predators in the meadow.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds — Red-tailed Hawk Life History
Cornell Lab All About Birds — Red-tailed Hawk Overview

records.name: Barn Owl
records.diet: Almost entirely small mammals — voles, mice, and shrews; hunted at night
records.shelter: Nests in tree hollows, cliff crevices, and quiet building cavities
records.preferredHabitat: Open grasslands and meadows hunted on silent wings at night
records.fact: A Barn Owl's heart-shaped facial disc funnels sound so precisely it can catch prey in total darkness by ear alone.

requirements.hint: A quiet, healthy meadow with plenty of voles and a dark place to roost.

records.role: The meadow's night-shift rodent hunter, coursing low over the grass on silent wings and swallowing voles and mice whole. This makes it a major check on rodent populations. In the meadow it sits near the top of the food web with no regular predators.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds — Barn Owl Life History

records.name: Tree Squirrel
records.diet: Acorns, nuts, seeds, tree buds, and fungi; occasional insects and bird eggs
records.shelter: Tree cavity dens and leaf-and-twig dreys built high in the canopy
records.preferredHabitat: Mature deciduous or mixed forest rich in oaks and hickories
records.fact: Gray squirrels scatter-hoard thousands of nuts each year, and the caches they forget grow into new trees.

requirements.hint: A nesting tree and fallen logs with seeds to cache.

records.role: Tree squirrels are major seed predators and accidental seed dispersers whose buried, forgotten nuts regenerate the forest canopy. They also spread mycorrhizal fungal spores and occasionally raid bird nests. As abundant prey they feed nearly every forest mesopredator and raptor.

records.name: Woodpecker
records.diet: Mostly insects—beetle larvae, ants, caterpillars—with some berries, seeds, and sap
records.shelter: Self-excavated cavities in standing deadwood; roosts in cavities year-round
records.preferredHabitat: Open deciduous and mixed woodland with dead snags full of insects
records.fact: Downy woodpeckers are small enough to hammer into goldenrod galls for fly larvae that larger woodpeckers can't reach.

requirements.hint: Woodpeckers need standing deadwood — keep some snags up.

records.role: Woodpeckers regulate wood-boring beetles and bark insects, easing pest pressure on trees. Their abandoned cavities house nuthatches, wrens, and flying squirrels, making them ecosystem engineers. They feed hawks, owls, and nest-raiding squirrels and snakes.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds — Downy Woodpecker

records.name: Forest Salamander
records.diet: Small invertebrates: mites, springtails, spiders, beetles, ants, and earthworms
records.shelter: Under logs, rocks, and moist leaf litter; retreats into soil burrows
records.preferredHabitat: Cool, damp deciduous forest floor with abundant woody debris
records.fact: In some eastern forests the combined weight of these tiny lungless salamanders exceeds that of all the birds.

requirements.hint: Damp shaded logs and clean shallow water.

records.role: Red-backed salamanders are a keystone of the forest-floor detritus web, controlling the mites and springtails that break down leaf litter. Their huge collective biomass makes them a key food subsidy for snakes, birds, and small mammals. They breathe through their skin, so they signal forest moisture and soil health.

records.name: Great Horned Owl
records.diet: Mammals and birds—rabbits, voles, squirrels, chipmunks, skunks—plus reptiles and frogs
records.shelter: Adopts old hawk, crow, or heron stick nests in large trees; also snags and ledges
records.preferredHabitat: Mature forest broken by open ground, across nearly every biome
records.fact: Great horned owls are among the only predators that routinely kill and eat skunks, seemingly unbothered by the spray.

requirements.hint: Tall trees, quiet shelter, and prey animals already returned.

records.role: The great horned owl sits at the top of the nocturnal forest food web, with the most varied prey base of any North American raptor. It regulates rabbits, squirrels, chipmunks, and even other owls, so its loss lets prey populations surge. Adults have essentially no predators; only eggs and young are vulnerable.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds — Great Horned Owl

records.name: Black Bear
records.diet: Berries, nuts, grasses, and forbs; insects, fish, and carrion; fawns opportunistically
records.shelter: Dens in hollow trees, root masses, rock crevices, or dug cavities; hibernates in winter
records.preferredHabitat: Dense forest with thick understory and abundant berry and nut mast
records.fact: Black bear cubs are born during hibernation weighing under half a pound—the smallest newborns relative to adult size of any placental mammal.

requirements.hint: Bears return only to a richly restored forest: lots of berries, water, shelter, and space.

records.role: Black bears are generalist omnivores that disperse berry seeds, dig up and regulate colonial insects, and opportunistically take deer fawns and elk calves. As the most abundant large carnivore in North American forests, they link the mast, insect, and vertebrate food layers at once. Adults have essentially no natural predators.

records.name: Red Fox
records.diet: Rodents, rabbits, birds, and reptiles; insects, fruit, and carrion
records.shelter: Earthen dens dug into slopes or taken over from other animals, reused for generations
records.preferredHabitat: Forest edges and scrub-woodland mixes; avoids dense unbroken forest
records.fact: Red foxes have around 28 distinct calls, and each individual's voice is recognizable to other foxes.

requirements.hint: Denning cover and small prey back in the woods.

records.role: The red fox is a versatile mesopredator that keeps small rodents, rabbits, and ground-nesting birds in check while dispersing seeds through the fruit it eats. It sits below apex predators like bears and bobcats and above the small mammals it hunts. Fox pairs often reuse and expand the same den site across generations.

sources.name: National Wildlife Federation — Raccoon (fox as predator)

records.name: Mule Deer
records.diet: Browser: leaves, twigs, and forbs in summer; woody browse, acorns, and berries in winter
records.shelter: No fixed den; beds in dense shrubs and forest cover for warmth and safety
records.preferredHabitat: Forest edges and open woodland with shrubby browse and water
records.fact: A bounding mule deer releases an alarm scent from its hind legs that alerts every nearby deer at once.

requirements.hint: Shrubby browse and a quiet pond.

records.role: Mule deer are key large browsers that shape the forest understory and the regeneration of shrubs and young conifers. They form a critical prey base for large carnivores, while their fawns feed bobcats, foxes, and bears. Seasonal migrations move nutrients across the landscape.

records.name: Elk
records.diet: Grasses, sedges, and forbs in summer; woody browse and bark in winter
records.shelter: No fixed shelter; calves hidden in dense vegetation; the herd shares vigilance
records.preferredHabitat: Grassy clearings and open woodland edges within larger forest
records.fact: In Yellowstone, elk make up about 85% of winter wolf kills and their carcasses feed at least a dozen scavenger species.

requirements.hint: Grassy clearings and water in a healthy forest.

records.role: Elk are a dominant large herbivore whose heavy grazing shapes grasslands, willows, and aspen; their decline lets vegetation rebound. As the primary prey of wolves, cougars, and bears, they anchor the large-predator food web, and their carcasses sustain a broad scavenger guild. Migrations redistribute nutrients across elevations.

records.name: Raccoon
records.diet: Opportunistic: crayfish, insects, frogs, fish, small mammals, bird eggs, fruit, and nuts
records.shelter: Hollow tree dens preferred; also rock crevices, burrows, and structures
records.preferredHabitat: Moist forest near water for foraging and dabbling
records.fact: A raccoon's sensitive forepaws carry about four times more touch receptors than its eyes have light receptors.

requirements.hint: A den log near water to dabble in.

records.role: Raccoons are adaptable omnivores that regulate crayfish, frogs, and invertebrates while dispersing fruit seeds and preying on bird nests. Their high density makes them a major mid-trophic connector between the aquatic and forest webs. Coyotes, large owls, and bobcats keep them in the mesopredator tier.

records.name: Porcupine
records.diet: Strict herbivore: inner bark in winter; buds, twigs, leaves, and mast in warmer months
records.shelter: Rock dens, hollow logs, and tree canopies; reuses the same dens seasonally
records.preferredHabitat: Coniferous and mixed forest with trees offering edible bark
records.fact: The fisher is one of the only predators able to kill porcupines, flipping them to reach the quill-free belly.

requirements.hint: Trees to climb and brushy shelter below.

records.role: Porcupines are ecosystem engineers whose bark-stripping kills or deforms trees, creating snags for cavity nesters and diversifying forest structure. Their mast feeding competes with deer and squirrels. They are the main prey base for fishers and a supplemental meal for bobcats and bears.

records.name: Bobcat
records.diet: Obligate carnivore: rabbits, rodents, squirrels, and deer fawns; some birds and reptiles
records.shelter: Dens in hollow logs, brush piles, thickets, and rock crevices
records.preferredHabitat: Forest with dense understory, brushland, and rocky terrain
records.fact: In the eastern U.S. bobcat numbers rise and fall closely with the local cottontail rabbit supply.

requirements.hint: Bobcats follow plentiful prey and need rocky, brushy cover.

records.role: Bobcats are keystone mesopredators that suppress rabbits, rodents, and squirrels, easing browsing pressure on forest plants. As mid-level hunters they sit below cougars and wolves and above the small mammals they take. They help structure entire small-mammal communities.

records.name: Chipmunk
records.diet: Seeds, nuts, and fruit, plus insects, worms, slugs, fungi, and occasional bird eggs
records.shelter: Underground burrows up to 10 m long with nest and food-storage chambers
records.preferredHabitat: Mature deciduous forest with logs, stumps, and rocky cover
records.fact: Chipmunks don't truly hibernate—they wake through winter to eat from seed caches holding over a liter of food.

requirements.hint: Rocky cover and brush piles on the forest floor.

records.role: Chipmunks are important scatter-hoarders that disperse tree seeds and fungal spores, aiding forest regeneration. They eat many insects in summer and, as abundant prey, feed a wide guild of predators from weasels to owls. Their burrows aerate soil and shelter other small animals.

records.name: Nuthatch
records.diet: Insects and spiders in summer; seeds, acorns, and cached nuts through winter
records.shelter: Tree cavities and old woodpecker holes in mature hardwoods; also nest boxes
records.preferredHabitat: Mature deciduous and mixed forest with large oaks and hickories
records.fact: Nuthatches sweep smelly insects around their nest hole, apparently to mask their scent from squirrels.

requirements.hint: Live trees to forage and deadwood to nest in.

records.role: Nuthatches prey on bark-dwelling insects, including tent caterpillars and wood borers, helping check forest pests. By wedging and caching acorns and seeds in bark they aid short-distance seed dispersal. They bridge the insect and seed layers and serve as prey for hawks and owls.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds — White-breasted Nuthatch

records.name: Garter Snake
records.diet: Earthworms, amphibians, and slugs; also leeches, fish, insects, and small rodents
records.shelter: Communal winter dens in burrows and rock piles; hides under logs and rocks
records.preferredHabitat: Moist forest edges and riparian zones near ponds and streams
records.fact: Garter snakes are the main predator of the toxic rough-skinned newt, and some have evolved resistance to its poison.

requirements.hint: A sunny rock pile beside grassy hunting ground.

records.role: Garter snakes are generalist mid-web predators that suppress earthworms, slugs, amphibians, and small fish. In the Pacific Northwest they are the key check on rough-skinned newts, and their toxin resistance makes them a famous coevolutionary node. They are important prey for raptors, corvids, and larger predators.

records.name: Banana Slug
records.diet: Dead leaves, fungi, decaying matter, and animal scat; occasional live seedlings
records.shelter: Under logs and bark; seals into a mucus cocoon during dry spells
records.preferredHabitat: Cool, shaded, persistently moist Pacific forest floor
records.fact: Banana slugs pass viable seeds and fungal spores through their gut, seeding plants and mycorrhizal networks as they crawl.

requirements.hint: Keep the forest floor damp, mossy, and full of logs.

records.role: Banana slugs are primary decomposers that break down leaf litter and scat, returning nutrients to the soil. They disperse seeds and mycorrhizal spores, partnering with both plants and the fungal networks that feed forest trees. Their numbing mucus deters most predators, leaving garter snakes and shrews as the main consumers.

records.name: Beaver
records.diet: Bark and cambium of willow and aspen, plus aquatic plants
records.shelter: Stick-and-mud lodges with underwater entrances
records.preferredHabitat: Slow channels with mud banks and woody plants to fell
records.fact: Beaver dams create wetlands that store water and support hundreds of other species.

requirements.hint: Restored water channels, mud banks, and woody plants.

records.role: The wetland's ecosystem engineer. By felling trees and building dams, beavers flood new ponds, raise the water table, and create habitat that most other marsh species depend on.

records.name: River Otter
records.diet: Fish, crayfish, frogs, and other aquatic animals
records.shelter: Bank dens with underwater entrances
records.preferredHabitat: Clean water rich with fish and slow prey
records.fact: River otters can hold their breath underwater for up to eight minutes while hunting.

requirements.hint: Otters follow the fish. Restore clean water and den banks first.

records.role: An agile aquatic mesopredator that patrols channels for fish and crayfish. Otters keep fish and amphibian numbers in check and are a sign of clean, well-connected water.

records.name: Muskrat
records.diet: Mainly cattails, reeds, and roots; sometimes clams and small fish
records.shelter: Dome lodges woven from reeds, and bank burrows
records.preferredHabitat: Reedy shallows with abundant cattails
records.fact: Muskrats can stay underwater for up to 15 minutes on a single breath.

requirements.hint: Reeds to eat and build with, water to swim.

records.role: A mostly plant-eating rodent that clips reeds and cattails, opening water lanes used by ducks and other marsh life. It is important prey for mink and otters.

records.name: Mink
records.diet: Fish, frogs, crayfish, and small mammals like muskrats
records.shelter: Bank burrows, often taken over from muskrats
records.preferredHabitat: Brushy banks beside busy water
records.fact: Mink can swim up to 30 metres underwater when chasing prey.

requirements.hint: Bank shelter and plenty of small wetland prey.

records.role: A fierce semi-aquatic hunter that takes fish, frogs, and even muskrats. Mink are versatile mesopredators that help regulate small wetland prey.

records.name: Great Blue Heron
records.diet: Fish, frogs, and small aquatic animals; also voles and other birds
records.shelter: Colonial stick nests high in trees near water
records.preferredHabitat: Still shallows for slow, patient hunting
records.fact: A great blue heron can strike like lightning to spear a fish or snap up a vole.

requirements.hint: Shallow water with fish, reeds, and quiet nesting space.

records.role: The tall, patient sentinel of the shallows and a top predator of the wetland's fish community. It stalks slowly, then strikes faster than the eye can follow.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds - Great Blue Heron

records.name: Mallard Duck
records.diet: Seeds and aquatic plants, plus insect larvae, snails, and worms
records.shelter: Ground nests hidden in reedy water edges
records.preferredHabitat: Calm pools with reed cover
records.fact: Mallards can sleep with one eye open, resting half their brain at a time.

requirements.hint: Calm shallow water with reed cover.

records.role: A dabbling omnivore that tips forward to feed on seeds, plants, and small invertebrates. Its ducklings and eggs feed many marsh predators.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds - Mallard

records.name: Red-winged Blackbird
records.diet: Insects in summer, seeds and grain the rest of the year
records.shelter: Cup nests woven into standing reeds
records.preferredHabitat: Dense reed beds and cattail marsh
records.fact: Male red-winged blackbirds can hide or flash their scarlet shoulder patches at will.

requirements.hint: The thicker the reeds, the better.

records.role: An abundant, noisy marsh songbird that eats insects and seeds. Males fiercely defend reed-bed territories that may hold a dozen nests.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds - Red-winged Blackbird

records.name: Sandhill Crane
records.diet: Grains, tubers, insects, and small animals
records.shelter: Large ground mounds of marsh plants near standing water
records.preferredHabitat: Broad, quiet, restored marshland
records.fact: Sandhill cranes mate for life and choose partners through leaping, bowing dances.

requirements.hint: Cranes need a wide, quiet, well-balanced marsh.

records.role: A stately omnivore of open marsh that probes for tubers and grain and snaps up insects and small animals. Its presence signals a wide, healthy wetland.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds - Sandhill Crane

records.name: Painted Turtle
records.diet: Aquatic plants, insects, small fish, and carrion
records.shelter: Muddy pond bottoms; basks on logs
records.preferredHabitat: Still water with basking logs
records.fact: Painted turtles overwinter under the ice, taking in oxygen through their skin.

requirements.hint: Still water and a soft bank to bask on.

records.role: A basking omnivore that grazes plants and hunts insects and small fish, and cleans up carrion. Young are mostly carnivorous, shifting toward plants with age.

records.name: Chorus Frog
records.diet: Small insects and other tiny invertebrates
records.shelter: Shallow water and wet vegetation
records.preferredHabitat: Shallow pools ringed with reeds
records.fact: A chorus frog's comb-like call carries up to half a mile across the marsh.

requirements.hint: Shallow water, reeds, and insect life.

records.role: A tiny insectivore whose spring chorus fills the marsh. It eats small invertebrates and is itself vital prey for herons, mink, and snakes.

records.name: Tiger Salamander
records.diet: Worms, insects, small invertebrates, and even small vertebrates
records.shelter: Damp burrows near fishless breeding pools
records.preferredHabitat: Fishless pools with soft banks
records.fact: Tiger salamanders are among the largest land salamanders in North America.

requirements.hint: Quiet breeding pools with soft digging banks.

records.role: A voracious burrowing carnivore that hunts worms and invertebrates near breeding pools. Larvae grow in fishless water and can even turn cannibal.

records.name: Dragonfly
records.diet: Flying insects as adults; aquatic larvae eat mosquito larvae and tadpoles
records.shelter: Emergent reed stems; larvae live in the water
records.preferredHabitat: Clean water with reed perches
records.fact: Dragonflies catch up to 95% of the prey they chase, among Earth's best hunters.

requirements.hint: Clean water and reeds for the larvae to climb.

records.role: A top invertebrate predator both in the air and underwater. Adults hawk flying insects while aquatic nymphs devour mosquito larvae and tiny fish.

sources.name: Natural History Museum - Dragonflies: The ultimate hunters

records.name: Damselfly
records.diet: Small flying insects as adults; larvae eat aquatic invertebrates
records.shelter: Waterside vegetation; larvae among submerged plants
records.preferredHabitat: Calm, clean shallows
records.fact: Damselflies fold their wings together over the back at rest, unlike dragonflies.

requirements.hint: Calm, clean water with plants at the edge.

records.role: A slender aerial insectivore that snatches midges and mosquitoes with its legs. Its aquatic nymphs hunt tiny invertebrates and feed marsh fish and frogs.

records.name: Water Strider
records.diet: Insects and larvae trapped on the water surface; also scavenges
records.shelter: Still water surfaces among emergent plants
records.preferredHabitat: Any calm pool
records.fact: Water striders ride the surface on legs coated in thousands of tiny hairs.

requirements.hint: One calm pool is enough.

records.role: A surface-skating predator and scavenger that seizes insects trapped in the water film. It is easy prey for fish, frogs, and wading birds.

records.name: Freshwater Minnows
records.diet: Algae, plankton, insect larvae, and small invertebrates
records.shelter: Deeper pools and reed roots
records.preferredHabitat: Connected clean pools
records.fact: Minnow schools are the foundation that herons, otters, and mink all depend on.

requirements.hint: Connected clean pools with reedy cover bring fish back — and everyone who eats them.

records.role: The forage base of the wetland food web. These schooling fish graze algae and plankton and eat insect larvae, then feed nearly every predator in the marsh.
